title: Review: HIV/AIDS and viral diseases; Antibiotics and antibiotic resistance; Monoclonal antibodies and ELISA; Gas exchange surfaces and SA:V in organisms
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: IM06#t2 term and clue written for the game; IM06#t1 term and clue written for the game; IM08#t1 term and clue written for the game; IM08#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX01a#N.11a, IM06#N.7, IM07#N.20, IM08#N.3, EX01a#N.10, IM07#N.3, IM08#N.13, EX01a#N.7a, IM07#N.19, IM08#N.14. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Capsid
items.clue: Protein coat around the two copies of single-stranded RNA.

items.label: Reverse transcriptase
items.clue: Enzyme packed inside the HIV particle that copies viral RNA into DNA.

items.label: Monoclonal antibodies
items.clue: Identical binding proteins made in the laboratory by a single line of cells.

items.label: Antigen
items.clue: Molecule whose shape is complementary to the binding protein that attaches to it.

questions.stem: An amoeba gets all its oxygen by diffusion across its cell-surface membrane. Why could a mouse not get enough oxygen by diffusion across its body surface alone?

options.text: A mouse has a smaller total surface area than an amoeba, so less oxygen can cross into its body.
A mouse has a much lower SA:V, and most of its cells lie too far from its surface for diffusion to supply them.
A mouse's cells are each much larger than an amoeba's cell, so every cell needs more oxygen than diffusion delivers.
Diffusion of oxygen can happen only in water, so a mouse on land cannot use it at any surface.

questions.stem: A person with untreated HIV infection eventually becomes unable to produce antibodies against new pathogens, even though tests show that B-lymphocytes are still present in their blood in substantial numbers. Which statement explains this?

options.text: HIV infects and kills the B-lymphocytes that make the antibodies, so the cells that are needed for antibody production are no longer present in the blood.
Antibodies are secreted by the helper T-lymphocytes, so when HIV destroys these cells the production of all antibodies stops.
HIV infects and destroys all types of white blood cell, so every part of the immune system, including antibody production, fails at once.
HIV infects and kills helper T-lymphocytes, and without contact with an activated helper T-cell a B-lymphocyte cannot be activated to make antibodies.

questions.stem: Tuberculosis is treated with four antibiotics at once for the first two months. Each drug acts on a different target in the bacterium. Why is a combination used rather than a single drug?

options.text: A single drug would cure the infection if taken for long enough; four are used only to shorten the treatment.
The drugs cause the bacteria to mutate, and four drugs cause so many mutations that the bacteria die.
The patient becomes resistant to each drug in turn, so several are needed to keep at least one working.
A few bacteria may resist any one drug by chance, but one resisting all four at once is very unlikely.

questions.stem: A home pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies. Which statement explains how the test indicates pregnancy?

options.text: The antibodies bind progesterone, which is present in the urine at a high level only during a pregnancy.
The antibodies bind hCG released into the blood by the mother's pituitary gland when she becomes pregnant.
The woman's own antibodies against hCG appear in her urine and are captured on the test strip.
The antibodies bind hCG in the urine, and only an implanted embryo or its placenta produces hCG.

questions.explanation: Monoclonal antibodies specific to hCG bind it as urine flows along the strip and produce a coloured line. Only the embryo or placenta secretes hCG.

questions.stem: Use the data on the mouse, human and elephant. Which statement is supported by the data?

options.text: The mouse uses more energy each day than the elephant, since its rate per kg is far higher.
Each kg of body uses energy at about the same rate in all three, so total use is proportional to mass.
Each kg of mouse uses energy about 13 times as fast as each kg of elephant.
The elephant has the highest rate per kg, because its greater surface area loses more heat.

questions.explanation: 720 ÷ 56 ≈ 13. The small mouse has a high SA:V, loses heat fast per kg, and so respires fast per kg.

questions.stem: Why do antibiotics fail to control infections caused by viruses?

options.text: Viruses are far smaller than bacteria, so antibiotic molecules are too large to bind to them or to enter them effectively.
Antibiotics would destroy the human cells inside which viruses replicate, so they cannot safely be used against a viral infection.
Viruses have no metabolic processes of their own; they use those of the host cell, which antibiotics do not block.
They do not fail: antibiotics kill viruses as well as bacteria, only more slowly, so a longer course is needed for a viral infection.

questions.explanation: A virus has no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism. It reproduces using the host cell's processes, which antibiotics leave untouched.

questions.stem: A company tests a new monoclonal antibody treatment. Which trial design gives the most reliable evidence that the treatment works?

options.text: Give the treatment to all patients this year and compare them with last year's untreated patients.
Randomly allocate patients to treatment or placebo; neither patients nor doctors know which.
Give the treatment to volunteers who expect to benefit, and record how much better they feel.
Run many small trials and publish those in which the treatment worked.

questions.explanation: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial removes bias in who is treated and in how results are judged.

questions.stem: Why does gas exchange become a greater challenge as organisms increase in size?

options.text: The surface area-to-volume ratio increases, so far more gas has to cross each unit of the exchange surface.
The surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, and the distance from the centre of the organism to its exterior increases.
Only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases, so the challenge arises once an organism is big enough to have them.
A large organism uses more oxygen in total; the distance gases must diffuse to reach its cells makes no difference.

questions.explanation: Proportionally less surface supplies each unit of volume, and inner cells are too far away for diffusion alone. Both make specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems necessary.

questions.stem: A clear zone has a diameter of 18 mm. What is its area, to 3 significant figures?

options.text: 1020 mm²
254 mm²
56.5 mm²
28.3 mm²

questions.stem: A rapid test for virus X has monoclonal antibodies complementary to protein N of virus X, on mobile coloured particles and fixed at the test line. The control line works as in a pregnancy test. A person infected with virus Y, whose protein N has a different shape, uses the test correctly. What result is expected?

options.text: Lines at C and T, because viruses X and Y both have a protein called N.
No lines at all, because no antigen binds, so the coloured particles do not move.
A line at C only: the antibodies cannot bind virus Y's protein N.
A line at T only, because antibodies bind any foreign protein that passes them.

questions.explanation: Virus Y's protein N is not complementary to the antibodies, so nothing is caught at T. The C line shows the test worked.
